fyNote: Financial year ends 31 December. Income statement rebuilt from the value-added statement; see the workbook for the balancing line.
segmentNote: Four businesses; tankers (Petroleum & Products) earn the most revenue and profit (AR p.54).

how.title: How MISC makes money
how.text: Revenue = long-term charter fees for ships and floating production units + freight from shorter voyages + shipyard project work

story.scale_label: ships, gas carriers, offshore units and a shipyard

items.label: Goods and services bought
items.tip: Fuel, port charges, crew services, ship repairs and shipyard materials.

items.label: Depreciation and impairment
items.tip: Wear and tear on ships and offshore units, plus write-downs of older vessels.

items.label: Employment costs
items.tip: Salaries for seafarers, yard workers and office staff.

items.label: Other items
items.tip: Items not split out in the value-added statement (balancing figure).

items.label: Tax
items.tip: Low, because shipping income is largely tax-exempt in Malaysia.

items.label: Profit to shareholders
items.tip: What is left for shareholders: paid as dividends or kept to grow the business.

pnl.incomeNote: Plus about RM12.36 per RM100 of revenue from other income (including an insurance recovery), interest, ship sales and a gain on buying an FPSO.

fiveYear.note: Revenue fell in 2025 mainly because heavy engineering projects finished and some gas carrier contracts ended; profit rose on the new FPSO and lower impairments.

rows.name: Petroleum & Products (AET tankers)
rows.tip: Oil and product tankers and shuttle tankers; earned more in 2025 on higher freight rates.

rows.name: Gas Assets & Solutions
rows.tip: LNG and ethane carriers on long charters, mostly to PETRONAS; lower after contract expiries and vessel lay-ups.

rows.name: Offshore
rows.tip: Floating production units (FPSOs) leased to oil companies; jumped as a new FPSO in Brazil started work.

rows.name: Marine & Heavy Engineering
rows.tip: Shipyard building offshore platforms and repairing ships in Pasir Gudang, Johor.

segments.note: Profit here is segment operating profit. Segment revenues add to slightly more than group revenue because of inter-segment sales.

assets.label: Ships, FPSOs, receivables and other assets

balance.note: Most of what MISC owns is ships and offshore units, many on long contracts. Assets and equity shrank in 2025 mainly because a weaker US dollar lowered their ringgit value (AR p.73).

safety.label: Cash from operations FY2025
safety.plain: Up 32% from RM4,277m, helped by better collections from customers.

safety.label: Borrowings
safety.plain: Down from RM15,494m after repaying USD400m of notes in April 2025 and a weaker US dollar.

safety.label: Net debt to equity
safety.plain: Borrowings minus cash are only a fifth of shareholders' funds: low for a shipping company.

safety.label: Interest cover
safety.plain: Earnings before interest and tax cover interest costs about 4 times.

safety.label: Dividends paid in 2025
safety.plain: Cash returned to shareholders during the year.

safety.label: Committed capital spending
safety.plain: Ships and projects already ordered or contracted, to be paid over coming years.

safetyTitle: Cash and debt at a glance
safetyIntro: MISC's integrated report gives these cash and debt figures; the full cash flow statement is in its separate audited accounts. Tap a card to see what it means.

metrics.label: Market value
metrics.plain: What the whole company costs at today's share price: RM34.5 billion.

metrics.label: P/E (FY2025 profit)
metrics.plain: You pay about RM20 for every RM1 of yearly profit. A high number means investors expect growth.

metrics.label: EPS (FY2025)
metrics.plain: Profit earned for each share you own over the year.

metrics.label: Dividend yield (FY2025 dividends)
metrics.plain: For every RM100 of shares, about RM4.9 a year comes back as cash dividends.

metrics.label: Payout ratio FY2025
metrics.plain: Of every RM100 profit, about RM100 is paid out; the rest is kept to grow.

metrics.label: Price to book
metrics.plain: The share price is 1.0 times the accounting value of what shareholders own.

metrics.label: Return on equity FY2025
metrics.plain: For every RM100 shareholders have in the company, it earned about RM5 profit last year.

metrics.label: Net margin FY2025
metrics.plain: What is left as profit for shareholders from every RM100 of revenue: RM15.25.

metrics.label: Revenue growth FY2025
metrics.plain: Revenue compared with the year before.

metrics.label: Profit growth FY2025
metrics.plain: Profit to shareholders compared with the year before.

metrics.label: Net debt
metrics.plain: Borrowings minus cash: RM6.78 billion owed to lenders after using all its cash.

metrics.label: Net gearing
metrics.plain: Net debt is 20% of shareholders' funds. Under 50% is usually seen as comfortable; above 100% means lenders fund more than owners.

metrics.label: Interest cover
metrics.plain: Earnings before interest and tax cover interest costs about 4 times (AR p.75).

drivers.evidence: Revenue is anchored on contracted, recurring income with selective spot exposure (AR p.16)
drivers.why: Makes earnings steadier than most shipping companies.

drivers.evidence: Long-term charters for five newbuild LNG carriers with PETRONAS LNG secured in early 2026 (AR p.14)
drivers.why: Locks in income for many years once the ships are delivered.

drivers.evidence: FPSO Marechal Duque de Caxias started operating; Offshore operating profit rose from RM52m to RM865m (AR p.74)
drivers.why: A large new earner for the Offshore business.

drivers.evidence: Gas segment revenue fell from RM2,987m to RM2,095m on contract expiries, lay-ups and lower charter rates (AR p.51, p.73)
drivers.why: Older ships without new charters earn less.

drivers.evidence: Heavy engineering revenue fell 45% as projects neared completion (AR p.74)
drivers.why: Lumpy: depends on winning and starting new projects.

drivers.evidence: Petroleum & Products revenue rose on higher freight rates and more earning days (AR p.73)
drivers.why: Rates can swing quickly with global oil trade.

drivers.evidence: Management says escalation is affecting energy supply chains, trade routes and freight markets (AR p.31)
drivers.why: Can lift freight rates but raises operating and safety risk.

drivers.evidence: A stronger ringgit cut the ringgit value of assets and equity (AR p.73)
drivers.why: Most income is in US dollars.

drivers.evidence: Repaid USD400m of notes; net debt/equity 0.20x; interest cover 3.9x (AR p.73, p.75)
drivers.why: A strong balance sheet to fund new ships.

drivers.evidence: RM7.9bn of committed capital spending (AR p.73)
drivers.why: Uses cash now for income later.

drivers.evidence: IMO net-zero rules delayed to October 2026; EU rules advancing (AR p.33)
drivers.why: May require cleaner, costlier ships, but also creates demand for new-energy shipping.

drivers.evidence: Dividend raised to 38 sen from 36 sen (AR p.73)
About 20 times FY2025 profit and about 1 times book value at RM7.72 (see Valuation)
drivers.why: Investors pay for steady contracted income.

competitors.name: Large shipping and LNG carrier owners (e.g. NYK, MOL, K Line, Teekay)
competitors.how: Compete for long-term gas and oil shipping charters
competitors.source: General market knowledge, not the report

competitors.name: FPSO contractors (e.g. SBM Offshore, MODEC, BW Offshore)
Regional shipyards in Singapore, Korea and China
competitors.how: Compete for offshore fabrication and ship repair

outlook.text: Entered 2026 with encouraging momentum: five new LNG carrier charters with PETRONAS and an FSO contract with ExxonMobil in Papua New Guinea (AR p.14).
First carbon-dioxide carrier charter secured, an entry into carbon transport (AR p.14).
2026 priorities: disciplined leverage, liquidity planning and spending on committed projects and fleet renewal (AR p.16).
Risks named: interest-rate uncertainty, geopolitical fragmentation and the Middle East conflict affecting trade routes (AR p.16, p.31).

outlookOverall.text: Management says MISC entered 2026 with encouraging momentum and new long-term contracts (AR p.14).
